canonical_statement: The study evaluates how memory substrate choice affects task performance and efficiency across user-centric question answering and agent-centric decision-making under a controlled shared harness.

The evaluation-landscape survey included 52 memory-augmented LLM systems released between early 2023 and April 2026 that proposed a memory method, reported at least one memory benchmark, and had a public preprint.

population.label: 52 memory-augmented LLM systems released early 2023 through April 2026

canonical_statement: In the 52-system landscape survey, 62% of benchmark-system usage was concentrated in LoCoMo and LongMemEval.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: percentage of benchmark-system pairs concentrated in LoCoMo and LongMemEval

canonical_statement: In the 52-system landscape survey, only 21% of systems reported any efficiency metric.
In the 52-system landscape survey, 81% of systems used GPT-family models as their sole backbone.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: systems using GPT-family as sole backbone

canonical_statement: The controlled harness implements 11 memory methods spanning seven substrate families, divided between external stores and internal weight or activation mechanisms.
M1 Dense Vector is a external flat index substrate in the harness. Dense embedding index with cosine-similarity top-k retrieval; no auxiliary LLM on write or read.
M2 Sparse Vector is a external flat index substrate in the harness. BM25 inverted index with sparse top-k retrieval; no auxiliary LLM.
M3 Gist Index is a external text record substrate in the harness. Auxiliary LLM creates page gists; an LLM selects gists/pages for expansion at read time.
M4 Evolving Notes is a external structural substrate in the harness. LLM writes linked notes and evolution-triggered neighbor rewrites; read uses ANN plus link expansion.
M5 Dual-Level Graph is a external structural substrate in the harness. LLM extracts entities and relations into a graph combined with vector retrieval.
M6 Hierarchical Tree is a external hierarchical substrate in the harness. LLM organizes memory into a four-level hierarchy with collapsed-tree dense retrieval.
M7 Distilled Strategies is a external refinement substrate in the harness. Trajectories are judged and distilled into reusable strategies, then top-1 strategy is retrieved.

M8 Skill Bundles is a external refinement substrate in the harness. Experiences are clustered, summarized, merged, and pruned into skill bundles; the study uses a zero-shot LLM controller with all bundles prefilled.
M9 Adapter Tuning is a internal weight substrate in the harness. An auxiliary LLM synthesizes QA pairs and a LoRA adapter is fine-tuned with answer-only loss.
M10 Full Context is a internal activation substrate in the harness. The full history is concatenated at read time, with oldest entries truncated at the context-window limit.

M11 Episode-Clustered Re-prefill is a internal activation substrate in the harness. Turns are clustered into episodes, budgeted to 25% of tokens, matched by centroid, and the best episode is re-prefilled at read time.
LoCoMo contributes 10 multi-session dialogues with 1,986 questions across five categories to the user-centric evaluation.

MemoryAgentBench is evaluated through Accurate Retrieval using LongMemEval-S, Long-Range Understanding, Test-Time Learning, and Conflict Resolution; Conflict Resolution is also used for context-length scalability testing.
ALFWorld contributes 134 valid-unseen embodied-planning tasks evaluated in within-episode and cross-episode regimes.
BigCodeBench-Hard contributes 148 code-generation tasks graded by execution with retrieval over a cross-task pool of successes and failures.
The harness evaluates Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B-AWQ, and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-IT with vLLM on four H200 GPUs and fixes gpt-4o-mini as the auxiliary LLM and LLM judge where required.
The harness instruments 26 performance and efficiency metrics, including benchmark-native performance plus storage, latency, token, call, total-time, and cost measures.
The retrieval-breadth ablation sweeps k={1,2,5,10,20} on LoCoMo and k={1,2,3,4,5} on ALFWorld against an otherwise identical no-memory prompt with an empty retrieved block.
The scalability ablation evaluates MAB Conflict Resolution at 6K, 32K, and 262K input tokens while holding the question pool, gold answers, and judge constant.

M7 is only evaluated on trajectory-bearing agent-centric tasks, M9 is incompatible with the Gemma A4B MoE routing, and M10 is omitted from both agent-centric benchmarks because cumulative context exceeds the tested windows.
For ALFWorld, the nearest retrieval-bank episode had mean cosine similarity 0.879 to evaluation tasks versus 0.068 for random bank episodes.
For BigCodeBench-Hard, the nearest retrieval-bank item had mean cosine similarity 0.594 to evaluation tasks versus 0.061 for random bank items.
On LoCoMo with Gemma-4-26B-A4B-IT, M5 Dual-Level Graph achieved P4 0.719 with 25.95 seconds per query.
On LongMemEval-S with Gemma-4-26B-A4B-IT, M5 Dual-Level Graph achieved P4 0.667 with 190.93 seconds per query.
On MAB Long-Range Understanding with Qwen3-8B, M10 Full Context achieved P4 0.676 with 6.58 seconds per query.
On MAB Test-Time Learning with Qwen3-32B-AWQ, M3 Gist Index achieved P4 0.850 with 94.29 seconds per query.
On MAB Conflict Resolution with Gemma-4-26B-A4B-IT, M5 Dual-Level Graph achieved P4 0.550 with 8.23 seconds per query.
Across the user-centric benchmarks, no single substrate wins every capability; M5 leads LoCoMo and LME-S across model bands, while the leaders change on MAB LRU, TTL, and CR.
M2 is consistently inexpensive, while M5 can be 10 to 100 times slower and is only worthwhile when its structural mechanism matches the task bottleneck.
On ALFWorld with Qwen3-8B, M11 Episode-Clustered Re-prefill achieved 11.9% task success versus 5.7% for NoMem.
On ALFWorld with Qwen3-32B-AWQ, M7 Distilled Strategies achieved the table-high task success rate of 32.1% versus 22.4% for NoMem.
On BigCodeBench-Hard with Qwen3-8B, M5 Dual-Level Graph achieved 15.5% Pass@1 versus 8.1% for NoMem.
On BigCodeBench-Hard with Gemma-4-26B-A4B-IT, M5 Dual-Level Graph achieved 20.9% Pass@1 versus 14.2% for NoMem.
On BigCodeBench-Hard with Qwen3-32B-AWQ, M2 Sparse Vector achieved 19.6% Pass@1 versus 16.2% for M5 at roughly one-sixth the latency.
ALFWorld favors memory mechanisms that denoise or abstract prior experience before it reaches the policy, whereas BigCodeBench-Hard generally benefits from broad retrieval of reusable code context.
On the Qwen3-32B-AWQ performance-latency frontier, M7 improved ALFWorld task success by 9.7 percentage points at 1.23 times NoMem latency overhead.

canonical_statement: On the Qwen3-32B-AWQ performance-latency frontier, M2 improved BigCodeBench-Hard Pass@1 by 2.0 percentage points at 1.28 times NoMem latency overhead.
Increasing retrieval depth monotonically increased LoCoMo P4 across tested substrates, while increasing retrieval depth reduced ALFWorld task success.
For M7 on ALFWorld with Qwen3-32B-AWQ, task success fell from 32.1% at k=1 to approximately 25% at k=5.

canonical_statement: In the MAB Conflict Resolution scalability sweep with Qwen3-32B-AWQ, M8 P4 increased from 0.32 at 6K tokens to 0.51 at 262K tokens while latency grew from about 1 second to about 10 seconds.

canonical_statement: On a full LoCoMo run, MemGPT used 2,739 auxiliary LLM calls and 16.3 hours, Mem0 used 8,984 calls and 11.8 hours, and Zep used 7,624 calls and 23.1 hours.

population.label: Full LoCoMo run with 10 conversations and 1,986 queries

canonical_statement: MemGPT, Mem0, and Zep were excluded from the main controlled comparison because their auxiliary-LLM budgets were one to two orders of magnitude above lighter substrates; the study reports them only as a production-cost reference.
M8 deviates from MemSkill by replacing its PPO-trained controller with a zero-shot LLM that consumes all refined skill bundles.
M11 deviates from EpiCache by replacing in-place KV-cache edits with utterance-level re-prefill because Qwen3 hybrid attention is unsupported by the released kernels.
The preprint states that code will be made available upon acceptance; the evaluated code is therefore not reported as publicly available in this version.
The authors conclude that substrate routing is necessary because the optimal memory substrate changes with task regime, retrieval depth, and history scale.
The authors propose a design rule to trade read breadth for write depth and argue that universal agent memory should compose heterogeneous substrates rather than commit to one substrate.
